item.title: How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40k staff (397 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://element.io/blog/how-the-european-commission-rolled-out-matrix-to-more-than-40-000-staff/, See on Hacker News

The European Commission went from a Matrix proof of concept in December 2025 to a sovereign communication tool rolled out to every Commission laptop by September 2026. That tool, built on Matrix by Element, and run by the Commission itself, now serves more than 40,000 users.

At The Matrix Conference 2026, Diana Gheorghe, Head of Sector for Digital Workplace Communication and Collaboration Services, and Alexandru Vignide, Service Delivery Manager for the Commission's sovereign communication tool, told the story of how they got there. The pair were transparent about what got harder at scale, and how they dealt with it.

Sovereignty means more than where the servers sit

“Sovereignty” can have a different meaning for different people and organisations, so the Commission started by pinning down what it means for them. Their answer spans five dimensions: resilience and business continuity, vendor diversity, control over their data, ownership of the platform, and leverage in procurement - the ability to negotiate with, or walk away from, a supplier. That last one is easy to forget, and arguably the one that bites hardest when it's missing.

For internal communications specifically, the priorities were resilience, data ownership and, crucially, interoperability. That's what led them to Matrix: an open protocol whose value lies in letting separate systems talk to each other. They chose Element Server Suite Pro (ESS Pro), Element's enterprise distribution of Matrix, as a mature implementation, and decided to host, operate and architect the service under their own control.

Sovereign cloud hosting, familiar login, without federation (yet)

With the building blocks chosen, Alexandru walked through three architecture decisions.

Hosting. The service doesn't run in a Commission-owned data centre. Instead it runs with sovereign cloud providers selected through the sovereign hosting tender awarded earlier this year, in order to meet its sovereignty and hosting requirements. Sovereign doesn't have to mean building everything in-house; it means choosing who you depend on, and on what terms.

Identity. The deployment is integrated with EU Login, the sign-in staff already use every day. A new tool is easier to adopt when logging in feels familiar.

Federation. Connecting to Matrix servers outside the Commission is still under assessment. The technical side is being explored - there was a separate hands-on demo using non-production environments at the conference - but federation also needs governance, participation and structure, which takes longer to agree than a config change.

Nine months from proof of concept to every Commission laptop

The Commission started working with Matrix in summer 2025, or, as Alexandru put it, at last year's Matrix Conference. From there, things moved quickly:

  1. December 2025: the architecture and engineering team delivered a proof of concept showing Matrix and Element were viable for the Commission. It earned a green light for a Commission-wide service, which Alexandru described as a nice Christmas present.
  2. January to June 2026: the team built the production infrastructure, along with the hosting and operations needed to run it, and was ready by June.
  3. Pilots: a laptop pilot covering both the desktop and web clients, followed by a mobile pilot through the Commission's mobile device management (MDM) platform.
  4. July to September 2026: the laptop rollout to all Commission users, delivered in waves, was and completed in September.

The Commission is now exploring a mobile rollout, and what federation could look like.

Scaling to 40,000 users brought challenges

Rolling out to 40,000 people surfaces problems no pilot will. Alexandru described the four main ones his team ran into, and how they tackled each.

Finding colleagues across servers. The Commission runs several Synapse homeservers, and early on, people on different servers couldn't always find each other. The Commission's teams worked with Element to fix this, and now a plain user search finds anyone in the Commission, whichever server they're on.

Accounts that only appear after sign-up. The Commission chose user-led account creation rather than pre-provisioning every account. The catch is that you can't find a colleague who hasn't registered yet, which made the discovery problem above feel worse while adoption was still ramping up.

Live presence was switched off. As more users came on board, the load from live presence (the real-time “online/away” indicator) started to affect performance, so the team disabled it. They're now looking at a user status feature being developed with Element as the replacement.

Infrastructure had to learn to scale itself. Rolling out in waves over three months meant uneven, shifting demand, so the team tuned the infrastructure to adjust automatically.

Running through all of this was the balance between security and usability. Most of the hardening work was done with the Commission's security teams before the rollout, and continues through regular security reviews and continuous improvements. The team made sure that hardening didn't get in the way of everyday tasks like creating an account, recovering it or verifying a new device, and documented those steps clearly for staff. Feedback from tickets, internal forums and public channels is consolidated into prioritised goals for the Commission's own roadmap.

The most common question, Diana said, is whether Element is meant to replace Microsoft Teams, or consumer apps like Signal and WhatsApp. The short answer: neither, directly. Element is positioned as an internal communication tool for specific use cases - secure communication among them - where the Commission's existing stack doesn't fully meet its needs. Teams bundles communication, collaboration and a whole platform behind it, so there's no one-to-one swap to be had.

That makes expectation-setting part of the job. People naturally compare workplace tools with the apps they use at home and go looking for feature-for-feature matches. Diana's view is that this mindset is something to address head-on in any organisational change: Element is a tool in its own right, with its own feature set, that the Commission and Element can evolve together.

Part of the goal is to bring work conversations onto a tool the Commission controls. 

Federation goes beyond tech

The Commission has been interested in federation for a long time. The obvious starting point is other EU institutions, but it wouldn't stop there: the Commission also works closely with member states, governments and non-governmental organisations.

No decision has been made yet, and the Commission is taking it one step at a time. First comes the technical question of what the technology can actually do, because, as Diana put it, there's no point writing policies technology can't deliver. Then comes governance: who the partners would be, on what terms, with what scope, and how security and privacy are handled.

The Commission's Takeaways

Alexandru ended the talk by sharing what the deployment had taught the Commission.

Sovereignty is operational. It depends on operational control and the trustworthiness of the whole chain of partners, not just on where the service is hosted.

Adoption depends on everyday usability. Discoverability, onboarding support and everything around the product shape whether people use it.

Interoperability needs more than technology. It also needs clear structure, participation and governance.

He also noted that introducing a new communication tool has been a journey, and still is. Along the way, the Commission has relied on trustworthy service providers, and he described the collaboration with Element as a success.

item.title: What's New in PHP 8.6 (175 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.php.net/releases/8.6/en.php, See on Hacker News

Will be released on November 19, 2026

Faster, Safer, More Powerful.

PHP 8.6 is a major update of the PHP language, with new features including Partial Function Application, a new Duration class, a Polling API, and a new clamp() function

PHP 8.6 has not been released yet. It will be released on November 19, 2026.

Key Features in PHP 8.6

More expressive code, stronger types, and scalable I/O.

Partial Function Application

Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, returning a Closure that accepts the rest.

New \Time\Duration Class

The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch.

Polling API

Scalable I/O multiplexing using epoll, kqueue, and other native mechanisms, available to event loop libraries like ReactPHP and AMPHP.

New clamp() Function

Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range.

New SortDirection Enum

A standard, type-safe way to express sort order that can be shared across libraries.

Readonly Property Defaults

Allows readonly properties to declare default values, so fixed values no longer have to be assigned in the constructor.

Partial Function Application

Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, using ? and ... placeholders for the rest. The result is a Closure, and the function is only called once the remaining arguments are passed to it.

$versions = ['8.4', '8.5', '8.6', '8.7', '9.0'];

$supportsPfa = array_filter(
    $versions,
    fn ($version) => version_compare($version, '8.6', '>='),
);
$versions = ['8.4', '8.5', '8.6', '8.7', '9.0'];

$supportsPfa = array_filter(
    $versions,
    version_compare(?, '8.6', '>='),
);

New \Time\Duration Class

The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch. Its representation is independent of any time and timezone and can represent a range of more than 250 years with nanosecond precision. This makes it well-suited to represent timeouts or benchmark timings in an expressive way.

/**
 * All delays are in microseconds.
 */
function backoff(
    int $baseDelay,
    int $step,
    int $attempt,
): void {
    $delay = $baseDelay + ($step * (2 ** $attempt));

    // Wait at most 30 seconds.
    usleep(min($delay, 30_000_000));
}

// 1 second base delay, plus 100 milliseconds
// doubling with each attempt.
backoff(1_000_000, 100_000, $attempt);
use Time\Duration;

function backoff(
    Duration $baseDelay,
    Duration $step,
    int $attempt,
): void {
    $delay = $baseDelay->add($step->multiplyBy(2 ** $attempt));

    // Durations are comparable, so min() works directly.
    $delay = min($delay, Duration::fromSeconds(30));

    time_nanosleep($delay->seconds, $delay->nanoseconds);
}

backoff(
    Duration::fromSeconds(1),
    Duration::fromMilliseconds(100),
    $attempt,
);

// Preconfigure the delays using Partial Function Application.
$waitBeforeRetry = backoff(
    Duration::fromSeconds(1),
    Duration::fromMilliseconds(100),
    attempt: ?,
);
$waitBeforeRetry($attempt);

Polling API

The new Io\Poll API efficiently monitors many streams at once using the best mechanism available on each platform (epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll), without the scalability limits of stream_select(). It is designed as a common foundation that event loop libraries such as ReactPHP and AMPHP can build on.

$server = stream_socket_server('tcp://0.0.0.0:8080');
$clients = [];

while (true) {
    $read = [$server, ...$clients];
    $write = $except = null;

    // Based on select(), which typically can't handle
    // more than 1024 connections
    stream_select($read, $write, $except, null);

    foreach ($read as $stream) {
        if ($stream === $server) {
            $clients[] = stream_socket_accept($server);
            continue;
        }

        $data = fread($stream, 8192);

        if ($data === '' || $data === false) {
            $key = array_search($stream, $clients, true);
            unset($clients[$key]);
            fclose($stream);
        } else {
            fwrite($stream, $data);
        }
    }
}
use Io\Poll\{Context, Event};

$server = stream_socket_server('tcp://0.0.0.0:8080');

// Automatically uses epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll
$poll = new Context();
$poll->add(new StreamPollHandle($server), [Event::Read]);

while (true) {
    foreach ($poll->wait() as $watcher) {
        $stream = $watcher->getHandle()->getStream();

        if ($stream === $server) {
            $client = stream_socket_accept($server);
            $poll->add(
                new StreamPollHandle($client),
                [Event::Read],
            );
            continue;
        }

        $data = fread($stream, 8192);

        if ($data === '' || $data === false) {
            $watcher->remove();
            fclose($stream);
        } else {
            fwrite($stream, $data);
        }
    }
}

Stream Error Handling

Stream operations can now be configured to throw a StreamException or to fail silently instead of emitting warnings. Errors are reported as structured StreamError objects with a StreamErrorCode enum case, the wrapper name, and the affected path or URL, and can also be retrieved later with stream_last_errors() or passed to a custom error handler.

$config = @file_get_contents('/etc/app/config.json');

if ($config === false) {
    // Only an unstructured message string is available
    $error = error_get_last();
    log_error($error['message']);
}
$context = stream_context_create([
    'stream' => [
        'error_mode' => StreamErrorMode::Exception,
    ],
]);

try {
    $config = file_get_contents(
        '/etc/app/config.json',
        context: $context,
    );
} catch (StreamException $e) {
    foreach ($e->getErrors() as $error) {
        // $error->code is a StreamErrorCode enum case
        log_error(
            $error->code->name,
            $error->message,
            $error->wrapperName,
        );
    }
}

New clamp() Function

Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range. Otherwise, the nearest boundary value is returned.

var_dump(max(0, min(-10, 100)));
// int(0)

var_dump(max(0, min(50, 100)));
// int(50)

var_dump(max(0, min(110, 100)));
// int(100)
var_dump(clamp(-10, 0, 100));
// int(0)

var_dump(clamp(50, 0, 100));
// int(50)

var_dump(clamp(110, 0, 100));
// int(100)

// Any comparable value works with clamp(). This
// includes the new Duration class.
var_dump(clamp(
    \Time\Duration::fromSeconds(30),
    min: \Time\Duration::fromMinutes(1),
    max: \Time\Duration::fromMinutes(10),
)->seconds);
// int(60)

New SortDirection Enum

The SortDirection enum provides a shared, type-safe way to express sort order with its Ascending and Descending cases. Previously, every library had to define its own way of representing sort direction, resulting in a mix of incompatible integers, strings, booleans, and custom enums. Since SortDirection is built into PHP, libraries can accept it in their public APIs without needing adapter code.

Learn more about this feature in The PHP Foundation’s blog.

class QueryBuilder
{
    private array $orderBy = [];

    public function orderBy(
        string $column,
        int $direction = SORT_ASC,
    ): static {
        $this->orderBy[] = $column . ' ' . match ($direction) {
            SORT_ASC => 'ASC',
            SORT_DESC => 'DESC',
        };

        return $this;
    }
}

$qb->orderBy('name', SORT_DESC);
$qb->orderBy('name', SORT_STRING);
// Accepted by the signature, then fails inside the method:
// UnhandledMatchError: Unhandled match case 2
class QueryBuilder
{
    private array $orderBy = [];

    public function orderBy(
        string $column,
        SortDirection $direction = SortDirection::Ascending,
    ): static {
        $this->orderBy[] = $column . ' ' . match ($direction) {
            SortDirection::Ascending => 'ASC',
            SortDirection::Descending => 'DESC',
        };

        return $this;
    }
}

$qb->orderBy('name', SortDirection::Descending);
$qb->orderBy('name', SORT_STRING);
// TypeError: QueryBuilder::orderBy(): Argument #2 ($direction)
// must be of type SortDirection, int given

Function and method parameters can now have their own DocComments, which are available via the new ReflectionParameter::getDocComment() method. This allows each parameter to be documented right next to its declaration, without repeating its name and type in a @param tag.

class DB
{
    /**
     * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query.
     *
     * @param string $query Terms to search
     * @param int $limit Maximum number of results
     */
    public function search(string $query, int $limit = 10): array
    {
        return [];
    }
}

// Parameter descriptions can only be extracted
// by parsing the function's DocComment.
class DB
{
    /**
     * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query.
     */
    public function search(
        /** Terms to search */
        string $query,

        /** Maximum number of results */
        int $limit = 10,
    ): array {
        return [];
    }
}

var_dump(
    new ReflectionParameter([DB::class, 'search'], 'query')
        ->getDocComment(),
);
// string(22) "/** Terms to search */"

New ReflectionProperty::isReadable() and ReflectionProperty::isWritable() Methods

With readonly properties, asymmetric visibility, and property hooks, checking whether a property is public is no longer enough to know whether it can be read or written. The new methods answer this directly for a given scope, and optionally for a specific object, taking into account visibility, initialization state, hooks, and magic methods.

class NewsEntry
{
    public string $title = 'PHP 8.6 released!';

    public private(set) string $slug = 'php-86-released';
}

$entry = new NewsEntry();
foreach (['title', 'slug'] as $item) {
    $property = new ReflectionProperty(NewsEntry::class, $item);
    printf(
        "%s: isReadable=%s isWritable=%s\n",
        $item,
        $property->isReadable(null, $entry) ? 'yes' : 'no',
        $property->isWritable(null, $entry) ? 'yes' : 'no',
    );
}
// title: isReadable=yes isWritable=yes
// slug: isReadable=yes isWritable=no

Readonly Property Defaults

Instance readonly properties, including those in readonly classes, can now declare a default value. This makes it simple to implement get-only interface properties with fixed values, which previously required assigning them in a constructor. The default counts as the property's initialization, so the constructor cannot overwrite it.

interface Rule
{
    public string $parser { get; }
}

final readonly class SlugRule implements Rule
{
    public string $parser;

    public function __construct()
    {
        $this->parser = SlugParser::class;
    }
}
interface Rule
{
    public string $parser { get; }
}

final readonly class SlugRule implements Rule
{
    public string $parser = SlugParser::class;
}

Additional Features and Improvements

  • The #[\Override] attribute can now be applied to class constants and enum cases.
  • Enums can now implement the __debugInfo() magic method.
  • Properties of objects stored in constants can now be modified directly, e.g. Config::DEFAULTS->timeout = 30.
  • New Uri\Rfc3986\UriBuilder and Uri\WhatWg\UrlBuilder classes build URIs from their components, along with new methods for detecting URI and host types and a Uri\WhatWg\url_percent_encode() function.
  • The Sodium extension adds post-quantum key encapsulation (X-Wing and ML-KEM-768), IP address encryption, and the SHAKE and TurboSHAKE extendable-output functions.
  • TLS streams now support session resumption, external pre-shared keys, and TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT).
  • New mysqli::quote_string() method escapes a string and wraps it in quotes, matching PDO::quote().
  • pack() and unpack() now accept the < and > endianness modifiers on integer and float format codes.
  • JSON error messages now include the location of the error in the input.
  • The new error_include_args INI setting consistently includes function arguments in error messages.
  • New grapheme_strrev() function reverses strings by grapheme cluster, and the new IntlNumberRangeFormatter class formats ranges of numbers.
  • New ZipArchive::openString() and ZipArchive::closeString() methods work with in-memory archives.
  • Performance improvements include compiling array_map() with first-class callable or partial application callbacks into loops, faster printf() calls, caching of stateless closures, and faster JSON encoding.

Deprecations and Backward Compatibility Breaks

  • Using return inside a finally block is now deprecated, as it silently discards exceptions and overrides values returned from the try or catch block.
  • Returning a value from __construct() or __destruct() is now deprecated, as is making them generators. Declaring a nullable return type for __debugInfo() is also deprecated.
  • Using let or is as the name of a class, function, or constant is now deprecated. Using _ as a constant name, namespace as a class constant name, or readonly as a function name is also deprecated.
  • The mbstring regular expression functions such as mb_ereg() and mb_split() have been deprecated, as the underlying Oniguruma library is no longer maintained. PCRE functions with the u modifier can be used instead.
  • The is_double(), is_long(), is_integer(), and doubleval() aliases have been deprecated. Use is_float(), is_int(), and floatval() instead.
  • spl_object_hash() has been deprecated in favor of spl_object_id(), and spl_classes() in favor of ReflectionExtension::getClassNames().
  • Passing an object where an array is expected to array_walk(), array_walk_recursive(), http_build_query(), mb_convert_variables(), and compression functions and filters is now deprecated. Use get_object_vars() to convert the object first.
  • strcoll() and the SORT_LOCALE_STRING sort flag have been deprecated. Use the Collator class from the intl extension instead.
  • Passing a third argument to define() is now deprecated, as is calling is_a() or is_subclass_of() with a class name string when $allow_string is false.
  • Using more than 16 filters in a php://filter URL without setting the filter.max_filter_count context option is now deprecated.
  • Sessions are now more secure by default: session.use_strict_mode and session.cookie_httponly are enabled, and session.cookie_samesite is set to Lax.
  • Custom session handlers that do not implement both create_sid() and validateId() are now deprecated.
  • The metaphone(), mysqli_get_charset(), and mysqli_stmt_init() functions are now deprecated, along with the CSV methods of SplFileObject and the sorting, flag, and serialization methods of ArrayIterator.
  • trim(), ltrim(), and rtrim() now also strip form feed (\f) characters by default.
  • fclose(), file_put_contents(), and copy() now return false when flushing or closing the stream fails, instead of silently ignoring the failure.
  • Many functions now throw a ValueError for out-of-range values, invalid flags, or strings containing NUL bytes, instead of silently truncating or ignoring them.

item.title: SSD prices will start going down the second half of next year (200 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.drivevault.io/blog/when-will-hard-drive-prices-come-down.html, See on Hacker News

It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog. So here is the straight answer: SSD prices should start to ease in the second half of 2027. Hard drives will take longer, probably into 2028, because the factories that make them have already sold that output.

That is not a guess. It comes from the analysts who track memory contract prices every quarter, and from what Seagate and Western Digital told their own investors this summer. Below we lay out the evidence, explain why spinning drives and SSDs are running on different clocks, and give you a realistic timeline with the signals to watch.

We have been following this since the start. Our April explainer on the storage price surge covered why prices took off. This article is the follow-up everyone keeps asking for: when does it end?

While you wait, the cheapest terabyte is the one you already own. DriveVault scans each of your external drives once and keeps a searchable catalogue of everything on them, so you can see free space, spot duplicate project folders and find old files without plugging anything in. For a lot of people that audit pushes the next drive purchase back by months, which is exactly what you want when prices are at a record.

Waiting for prices to fall? Use what you have first. DriveVault catalogues every drive you own so you can search them offline, find free space and spot duplicates before you buy.

Download Free

The short answer

SSDs and flash

Second half of 2027

NAND supply is forecast to catch up with demand from mid-2027. Expect a gradual slide, not a crash.

Hard drives

2028 at the earliest

Capacity is contracted into 2028 and no new factories are planned. Relief comes via bigger drives, slowly.

The Short Version

  • Prices are still rising, just more slowly. A year into the crisis, hard drives cost 134% more than in September 2025 and SSDs 129% more, in ComputerBase's tracking.
  • SSDs should turn first. TrendForce expects the NAND shortage to end in the second half of 2027.
  • Hard drives are booked up. Seagate has most of its data centre capacity allocated into 2028, and neither it nor Western Digital is building new factories.
  • 2024 prices are not coming back soon. Contracts now include pricing, and AI demand is still growing.
  • Need storage for work? Buy it. Buying speculatively? Wait, and favour SSDs, which should get cheaper first.

Where Prices Stand in September 2026

Before looking forward, it helps to be honest about where we are. The German tech site ComputerBase has priced the same dozen popular drives every month since mid-September 2025, which makes its tracker one of the cleanest before-and-after records of this crisis. Its one-year check, published today, shows hard drives averaging 134% above their pre-crisis prices, up from 129% a month earlier. SSDs are 129% higher, up from 126%. Both are new records.

DriveSept 2025Sept 2026Change
Seagate IronWolf 4TB (HDD)€94€195+108%
WD Red Plus 8TB (HDD)€170€349+105%
Toshiba MG09 18TB (HDD)€288€858+198%
Seagate BarraCuda 24TB (HDD)€308€804+161%
Kingston NV3 1TB (SSD)€50€144+189%
Samsung 990 Pro 4TB (SSD)€285€609+114%

Source: ComputerBase price check, 16 September 2026. German retail prices, excluding eBay and Amazon Marketplace sellers.

The pattern in that table matters. The biggest hard drives, the 18TB to 24TB models that data centres also buy, have risen fastest. The smaller desktop drives most creatives actually use have "only" doubled. If you are shopping for a budget external drive, you are feeling the mild end of this.

The one encouraging detail: the monthly increases have shrunk to a few percentage points. Prices are still climbing, but the curve is flattening. That is usually the first stage before a market turns.

Why Hard Drives and SSDs Will Recover at Different Times

Most coverage lumps "storage prices" together. That hides the most useful part of the answer, because hard drives and SSDs are made by different companies, in different factories, and sold in different ways.

SSDs follow the chip market

SSDs are built from NAND flash chips made by Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Those chips are priced quarter by quarter in contract negotiations, and some trade on a spot market that moves weekly. When supply catches up, SSD prices can respond within a couple of quarters. They went up fast. They can come down reasonably fast too.

Hard drives follow multi-year contracts

Hard drives come from essentially two companies, Seagate and Western Digital, with Toshiba a distant third. Almost all of their output now goes to cloud providers on long-term agreements. Those agreements lock in volume and, crucially, price for years at a time. That is why hard drive prices rose later and more steadily than SSDs, and it is why they will be slower to fall.

The SSD Timeline: What the Analysts Say

TrendForce is the most widely cited memory pricing firm, and its forecasts have been the best guide through this cycle. Here is how its view has shifted during 2026.

At the start of the year, it was forecasting NAND contract prices rising 33 to 38% in a single quarter, with client SSDs rising at least 40% as suppliers moved capacity to data centre drives. By July the tone had changed. Its third-quarter survey forecast a much smaller 10 to 15% rise for NAND, and said plainly that PC and smartphone makers had hit the limit of what they could afford to pay.

Then came the forecast that actually answers the question. In its July NAND update, TrendForce said the market would run a 4 to 5% supply deficit through 2026, then move back into balance in the second half of 2027. The reasons it gives are ordinary ones: manufacturers squeezing more bits out of existing fabs, steady output growth, and consumer demand staying weak because everything costs so much. It expects notebook shipments to fall around 10% this year and shrink again in 2027.

New supply is also arriving from China. YMTC reached around 14% of global NAND shipments in the second quarter and has told investors it wants to be the world's largest NAND maker by the end of 2027, backed by a planned $4.9 billion share listing. Even if it falls short of that target, that much extra flash entering the market is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes SSD prices down.

Balance is not the same as cheap. TrendForce also warns that memory contract prices will remain broadly elevated in 2027, with cloud providers' spending projected to rise another 50% next year. And it flags that a breakthrough in agentic AI could soak up the extra supply. A market in balance means prices stop rising and start drifting down. It does not mean a return to 2024.

You may also have seen SK hynix's chief executive say that 2027 will be the worst supply year in the industry's history. That sounds like it contradicts TrendForce, but it mostly does not. His comments are about memory overall, and the worst of the squeeze is in DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. TrendForce itself now describes a diverging market in 2027: DRAM staying tight while NAND eases. That is good news for SSDs and less good news for RAM, which is part of why Macs keep getting more expensive, as we covered in our piece on Apple's price rises.

The Hard Drive Timeline: Booked Into 2028

For spinning drives, the most reliable evidence is what the two big manufacturers said on their earnings calls this summer. It is not encouraging for anyone hoping for a quick drop.

Seagate reported its fiscal year results on 28 July, with a record 52.7% gross margin. On the call, management said data centres now take around 90% of the capacity it ships, and that the vast majority of its high-capacity drive output is now allocated into calendar 2028. Seagate also told investors it has contracts setting both product configuration and pricing for the whole of 2027, and that it is not adding drive manufacturing capacity. Its plan is to cram more data onto each disk instead.

Western Digital tells the same story. Its fourth-quarter revenue rose 44% year on year, while the amount of storage it shipped rose only 22%. The gap is price. According to analysis of the earnings call, the company's average price per terabyte rose by a high-teens percentage, and its long-term agreements run through 2027 with two major customers and through 2028 with one, with price terms attached.

Put simply: the companies are sold out, they are making record margins, their contracts fix prices into 2028, and they have chosen not to build more factories. None of those conditions produce falling retail prices.

So where does hard drive relief come from?

Density. Seagate's HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) drives already make up around 40% of its data centre capacity shipments, and Western Digital plans full-scale HAMR production in 2027. As the cloud giants move to 36TB, 40TB and larger drives, the cost per terabyte falls for everyone, and older production lines can eventually be freed up for the consumer and mid-capacity drives you and I buy. That is a slow, grinding process. It points to prices levelling off through 2027 and easing from 2028, rather than a sudden correction.

A Realistic Timeline

Pulling all of that together, here is our best reading of how the next two years should play out. Treat it as a forecast, not a promise. Every forecast in this cycle so far has been revised at least once.

  • Rest of 2026 Still rising, but slowly Small monthly increases for both hard drives and SSDs. Black Friday may bring a handful of genuine deals on specific SSDs, but no broad drop. The NAND market stays in deficit.
  • First half of 2027 The plateau SSD contract prices flatten as new flash supply builds. Hard drive prices hold at their peak under long-term contracts. DRAM remains very tight, so Macs and PCs stay expensive.
  • Second half of 2027 SSDs start to ease NAND supply and demand move into balance. Portable and internal SSD prices begin a gradual decline, with the largest capacities, which rose most, likely to fall most. Hard drives stay broadly flat.
  • 2028 onwards Hard drives follow As current contracts roll off and HAMR drives dominate data centres, hard drive cost per terabyte should improve. Prices should settle meaningfully below today's levels, but probably above 2024's.

What Could Change the Timeline

It could come sooner if AI infrastructure spending cools, Chinese NAND output ramps faster than expected, or consumer demand stays so weak that manufacturers start discounting to move stock. Module makers are already sitting on higher inventories because shoppers have stopped buying, which is the kind of pressure that eventually breaks prices.

It could come later if agentic AI takes off and data centres start storing far more data per user, if more manufacturers follow Micron's Crucial brand out of the consumer market, or if trade restrictions tighten on Chinese memory makers.

Signals worth watching

  • A flat or falling quarter in TrendForce's NAND contract survey. That would be the first since the crisis began, and the clearest sign SSD relief is on its way.
  • ComputerBase's monthly price check going negative for SSDs or hard drives. It publishes mid-month and is a good public scoreboard.
  • New SSD launches at the same or lower prices than the models they replace. The recent Samsung P9 and P7 did the opposite.
  • Seagate or Western Digital mentioning pricing pressure or customers delaying orders. So far, both say demand visibility is improving.

Should You Buy Now or Wait?

That depends entirely on why you need the storage. Here is how we would think about it.

You need storage for paid work this year

Buy now

Waiting has no clear end date, and a lost booking costs more than the price premium. Buy what the job needs, not more. Our 4TB drive roundup and rugged 4TB SSD guide focus on value at today's prices.

Your backups are incomplete

Buy now

A failed drive with no second copy is far more expensive than any price spike, especially when a replacement costs double. A basic spinning drive is still the cheapest way to hold a second copy. Just make sure the backup is actually complete. Our guide to verifying a backup drive shows how.

You want a fast SSD upgrade that can wait

Wait if you can

SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first. If your current setup works, holding off until the second half of 2027 is a reasonable bet. You are accepting the risk that prices plateau rather than fall.

You are stockpiling "just in case"

Don't

Buying spare capacity at record prices, to sit empty on a shelf, is the worst trade in this market. You would be paying the peak for storage you might not need until prices have eased.

Before You Buy Anything, Audit What You Have

The most useful thing you can do while prices are this high is find out exactly what is on the drives you already own. Most creatives with a few years of work behind them have a drawer of drives, a few with duplicate project folders, and at least one nobody is quite sure about. DriveVault turns that pile into a catalogue you can search in seconds, even when the drives are unplugged.

  • See real free space across every drive before assuming you need a new one.
  • Find duplicate folders across drives with drive comparison, and reclaim the space safely.
  • Confirm a backup is complete before you wipe and reuse the original drive.
  • Search files on unplugged drives, so shelved archives stay useful. Here is how offline search works.
  • Share the catalogue with your team so nobody buys a drive to hold footage that already exists. See sharing drive catalogues.

If you want a system for keeping it that way, our guide to organising multiple external drives covers naming, folder templates and archiving. Every terabyte you recover now is one you do not have to buy at 2026 prices.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will hard drive prices come down?

Probably not before 2028 in any meaningful way. Seagate says the vast majority of its data centre hard drive capacity is already allocated into calendar 2028, and Western Digital has long-term agreements with price terms running through 2027 and 2028. Neither company is adding factory capacity. Relief is more likely to come from higher-capacity HAMR drives lowering the cost per terabyte than from a sudden price cut.

When will SSD prices come down?

TrendForce expects the NAND flash market to stay in a 4 to 5 percent supply deficit through 2026 and to move back into balance in the second half of 2027. That makes late 2027 the earliest realistic window for SSD prices to start falling, with gradual easing rather than a sharp drop.

Will hard drive and SSD prices go back to 2024 levels?

Not within the next two years on current evidence. Manufacturers have signed multi-year contracts that include pricing, and AI data centres now account for most of their output. Prices should ease from their peak, but planning around a return to 2024 prices is not supported by any current forecast.

Should I buy a hard drive now or wait?

If you need the storage for paid work or your backups are incomplete, buy now, because waiting for hard drive prices has no clear end date. If you are buying extra capacity speculatively, SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first, from the second half of 2027. Either way, audit the drives you already own first, since duplicated files often free up more space than people expect.

Why are hard drives so expensive in 2026?

AI data centres are buying almost all of the high-capacity drives Seagate and Western Digital can build, under long-term contracts. Data centres now take around 90 percent of Seagate's shipped capacity. With consumer products a small slice of their business and no new factories planned, retail prices have more than doubled since September 2025 in ComputerBase's tracking.

The Bottom Line

Storage prices will come down. Just not yet, and not evenly. SSDs are on track to turn first, from the second half of 2027, as new flash supply catches up and consumer demand stays weak. Hard drives are locked into contracts that run into 2028, and their recovery will be slower and quieter, carried by bigger drives rather than price cuts.

The practical move for the next year is simple. Buy what you genuinely need, skip the stockpile, and get every usable terabyte out of the drives already on your desk. We will update this article as the forecasts change.

item.title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite (157 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://zerodha.tech/blog/high-performance-distributed-blob-storage/, See on Hacker News

TLDR; We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.

On Kite, our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes.

Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB (ssdb), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years.

Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement:

  1. SSDB became unmaintained, which was an obvious operational risk. It is written in C++, which is not a part of our stack or expertise, so forking and maintaining was also not viable.
  2. Scaling and size limits. SSDB is not a distributed system and can only run on a single node. This imposes significant future scaling challenges, including at one point forcing us to cap blob sizes at 1 MB because latency degrades on larger payloads.

As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were:

  • A key-value blob store with a simple API.
  • Designed for multi-megabyte blob read/write ops and high throughput. We sustain loads of thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second reading and writing arbitrary blobs. These are unpredictable and bursty thanks to the volatility in stock markets.
  • Horizontally scalable, distributed.
  • Disk-space efficiency / compression.
  • Easily maintainable and highly economical.

So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following:

  • ScyllaDB: We already run ScyllaDB for high-throughput workloads, but in our tests, it turned out to be suboptimal for large blobs. Significantly lower throughput and higher resource usage. We specifically want multi-megabyte blobs. Tombstones from frequent overwrites and TTL expiries require careful tuning in ScyllaDB.
  • PostgreSQL: We already have considerable experience with Postgres in our stack and experimented with storing blobs as BYTEA columns, but it turned out to be severely suboptimal again for the use case in terms of performance and disk-space efficiency.
  • YugabyteDB: Has blob storage as one of the options, but is not primarily designed or optimized for it. Also, a large system with too many features.
  • RocksDB: Had the right primitives, but again, not architected for high throughput multi-MB blob writes.
  • Ceph: Severe operational complexity and resource requirements. We didn’t even get to trying it out.
  • SeaweedFS: This was the closest candidate. However, there were a few blockers. Our use case is overwrite-heavy (a user changing their workspace) over the same key, and SeaweedFS keeps appending before compaction, which can cause disk usage to grow uncontrollably. Blobs have their own IDs, which then have to be mapped against user keys in a separate DB, adding another layer. It doesn’t support TTL per blob. Also, reasonably complex setup with many parts.
  • S3 and MinIO: Object storage has high per-request latency for small blobs, high request costs under write-heavy workloads (writes are 50% of our traffic), and coarse lifecycle TTLs instead of exact key expiry. Not to mention, S3 would incur significant costs given thousands of ops per second and tens of millions of ops per day.
  • Raw filesystem (one file per blob): Putting blobs directly on disk meant implementing atomic writes and write batching, managing large numbers of files and directories, good old atomic read/write disk performance and inode headaches, and maintaining a separate metadata index for TTLs. Not to mention, orchestrating this over AWS storage volumes.

Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its 35% Faster Than The Filesystem claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates millions of tables every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens?

So we ended up building Blobasaur, an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB.

What we needed

We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements:

  • Redis protocol compatibility (if possible at all): Every existing client already used standard Redis libraries (GET, SET, HGET, HSET, DEL, EXPIRE). If we could get a system that could be a drop-in replacement, that would allow us to leave existing services untouched and reduce risk significantly.
  • Low latency across payload sizes: It needed to serve both 2 KB settings blobs and 5 MB chart layouts with single-digit millisecond latency.
  • Built-in compression: Almost all our payloads are repetitive JSON, which compresses well.
  • Simple CRUD with TTLs: We didn’t need complex data structures, server-side scripting, or secondary queries. We just needed key-value and hash CRUD with key expiry.
  • Multi-node partitioning: We needed to split data across multiple machines so a single node wasn’t a bottleneck.
  • Relaxed durability is acceptable: This store holds non-critical UI and workspace preferences, and not critical financial data. If a sudden power loss drops recent writes, a user might lose a recent chart layout tweak, which is annoying, but it never affects trading. This was a good performance trade-off for our use case.

Why SQLite (and Rust)

We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves:

  • Atomic writes and batching.
  • TTL cleanup, which needs secondary indexes or walking the directories.
  • Dealing with fd limits.
  • Managing metadata separately from the raw data.

SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB.

Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard sqlite3 CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc.

While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust (sqlx, rusqlite, and tokio), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary.

Architecture

Splitting data into shards

In WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly.

To get write concurrency on a single machine, Blobasaur splits data across multiple SQLite database files on disk, called shards:

  • Consistent hashing: Each key maps to one shard via multi-probe consistent hashing.
  • Per-shard writer with group commit: Each shard has a dedicated writer task fed by a bounded queue. Instead of committing one key at a time, the writer drains a batch of pending writes from the queue and executes them inside a single BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT transaction. This amortizes transaction and WAL overhead across concurrent clients.
  • Concurrent readers: Reads go directly to a per-shard pool of read-only SQLite connections and can run concurrently with the writer.

How much does sharding help?

We benchmarked 1 shard against 16 shards using a load generator opening 64 concurrent connections. Each request used a 64 KiB JSON blob payload (close to our production average), which zstd compresses roughly 9x.

All runs used 100,000 keys, synchronous writes, and batch_size = 50, with the data directory on tmpfs to isolate SQLite locking and CPU overhead from disk variance. Both setups received the same total resources: 1,600 MB of SQLite page cache and 64 total read connections.

Workload1 shard16 shards
HSET only7,740 ops/s, p99 10.7 ms25,324 ops/s, p99 8.3 ms
50% HSET, 50% HGET14,227 ops/s, p99 10.5 ms29,538 ops/s, p99 8.5 ms
HGET only67,128 ops/s, p99 2.1 ms70,884 ops/s, p99 2.3 ms

With 16 shards, write throughput increases 3.3x and median write latency drops from 8.2 ms to 2.1 ms. Read throughput stays nearly identical because SQLite WAL mode already serves concurrent readers without contention.

At 25,324 HSET operations per second, each carrying a 64 KiB payload, Blobasaur processes roughly 1.66 GB/s of uncompressed JSON through zstd. Both the server and load generator ran on the same 16-core laptop, sharing its CPU resources.

Schema

Our services use both plain keys (SET/GET) and Redis hashes (HSET/HGET) to group blobs by service or feature (for example, HSET prefs userID <json>).

Inside each shard, plain keys live in a blobs table:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS blobs (
    key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    data BLOB,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    expires_at INTEGER,
    version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_expires_at
    ON blobs(expires_at)
    WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL;

SET writes to blobs. HSET writes to a table for its namespace, blobs_<namespace>, with the same columns. For example, HSET prefs user42 ... stores user42 in blobs_prefs.

Expiry is stored in expires_at on the same row. Read queries filter out expired rows at read time (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > ?), while a background worker reaps expired rows asynchronously. Because the index on expires_at is a partial index (WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL), rows without a TTL take up no space in the expiry index.

Compression

Blobasaur supports zstd, lz4, gzip, and brotli compression before writing to SQLite. We run zstd in production.

Here is the compression ratio across one hour of production HSET traffic:

HSET payloadSent by the clientStored in SQLiteReduction
Average63.6 KiB5.5 KiBabout 11x
p99935 KiB59.3 KiBabout 16x

With SQLite’s default 4 KiB pages, shrinking a 63.6 KiB payload to 5.5 KiB reduces its storage footprint from roughly 16 pages to roughly 2, before accounting for row and index overhead. Fewer pages holding blob data means less pressure on the page cache and less data to write through the WAL and into the database.

Durability

Because we don’t require strict durability for our specific use case of UI preferences, shards run in WAL mode with PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL. SQLite does not fsync on every transaction commit. An OS crash or power loss can lose recent committed transactions that have not yet been synced to durable storage, while preserving database consistency.

For workloads that want even lower write latency, Blobasaur also supports an optional async_write mode that acknowledges writes as soon as they enter the shard’s memory queue, before the SQLite batch commits.

Scaling across machines

To scale beyond a single server, Blobasaur implements the Redis Cluster protocol, making it compatible with standard cluster-aware Redis clients. Like Redis Cluster, the keyspace is divided into 16384 hash slots using CRC16. Each Blobasaur node owns a configured range of slots, and nodes discover each other via gossip. If a client sends a key to the wrong node, the node responds with a MOVED redirect pointing to the owner node.

This gives Blobasaur two-level routing:

  1. Cluster level: CRC16(key) % 16384 selects the machine.
  2. Node level: Multi-probe consistent hashing selects the SQLite shard on that machine.

There are some limitations right now. At present, slot assignment is static in config. Live slot rebalancing between running nodes and automatic failover are not implemented yet.

Changing the number of shards

We chose multi-probe consistent hashing so resharding a node only has to move minimal data, without needing virtual nodes. With naive hash % num_shards, increasing from 4 to 5 shards moves ~80% of keys. With consistent hashing, only ~20% of keys move (the share belonging to the new shard).

Resharding is currently an offline operation via the built-in CLI:

  1. Stop the server.
  2. Run blobasaur shard migrate 4 5 --verify.
  3. Update num_shards in config.toml and start the server.

The migration tool moves keys whose target shard changed. With --verify, it checks that keys are in the expected shards and reports post-migration row counts.

Moving off SSDB

We rolled out Blobasaur in a phased deployment strategy:

  1. New workloads first: When we launched Kite Terminal mode, we pointed its workspace storage directly at Blobasaur.
  2. Dual-write and backfill: For existing workloads like chart preferences, we updated the services to dual-write to both SSDB and Blobasaur while running a background migration for historical keys. Reads went to Blobasaur first and fell back to SSDB on a cache miss or error.
  3. Cutover: On the client side, the only code change was switching from a single-node Redis client to a Redis Cluster client with the three Blobasaur node IPs.

After running dual-writes for a month with zero discrepancies, we turned off SSDB.

What we learned along the way

Deleting rows doesn’t shrink SQLite files

Early on, we noticed disk usage only grew, even after millions of keys expired or were deleted. By default, SQLite keeps freed pages on an internal freelist for future writes rather than returning space to the OS.

To fix this, we enabled PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL across every shard and added a blobasaur shard vacuum subcommand to reclaim unused freelist pages within a set allocation (128 MB default). Since shrinking the actual database file in WAL mode requires a checkpoint, Blobasaur runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) right after executing an incremental vacuum.

Async writes have to be visible to every read

When async_write is enabled, a write returns OK while still sitting in the shard’s memory queue waiting for the next batch commit. To preserve read-your-writes consistency, queued writes are also placed in an in-memory pending map that reads check before querying SQLite.

During testing, we hit edge cases where certain read and existence-check paths bypassed this pending map or didn’t account for deletes. For example, a DEL followed immediately by a GET could return the old value from SQLite because the queued DEL hadn’t committed yet. We fixed this by storing explicit tombstones in the pending map and routing every read (GET, HGET, EXISTS, TTL) through it first.

In production, our p99 write latency normally sat below 5 ms, but we occasionally saw spikes to 30 to 50 ms.

We traced the spikes to the background TTL cleanup task. Initially, the cleanup worker opened its own write connection and ran a single large DELETE statement for all expired rows. That large DELETE contended with the shard’s main writer for SQLite’s single write lock, stalling normal client batches.

We fixed this in two ways: routing cleanup batches through the shard’s existing writer connection so they take turns cleanly with client writes, and bounding each pass with cleanup_chunk_size (1,000 rows by default). Since expired rows are already filtered out at read time, spreading physical deletion across smaller chunks eliminated the latency spikes without affecting correctness.

In production

Our current Blobasaur deployment runs as a three-node (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) cluster. Over a full trading session (09:00 to 15:30), p99 latency across all commands stays around 2 ms on every node, and p50 sits between 250 and 550 µs.

Broken down by command, HSET p99 sits around 2 ms, HGET p99 around 1.4 ms, and HDEL p99 mostly under 1 ms.

Blobasaur is open source under the AGPLv3 license and available on GitHub @iamd3vil/blobasaur. Find other projects from the Zerodha.tech hacker collective at 4th Cross Labs.

item.title: 15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP (268 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://kapteko.com/15-million-webservers/, See on Hacker News

Nov 18, 2026

Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there aren’t enough web servers for everyone. Let’s run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldn’t get funding, so we’re bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, I’ll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and we’ll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.

Web server

Instead of vibe coding it all, let’s use an ancient technique called learning. First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.

  1. listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socket
  2. accept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socket
  3. recv - receives data from a socket
  4. send - sends data
  5. close - closes

What is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Let’s use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.

int main(void)
{
    // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port
    int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); 
    if (listen(server, 128) < 0)
        return 1;
    const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK";
    for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) {
        if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0)
            send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        close(client);
    }
}

It couldn’t be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that we’ve learned everything, let’s finish the article and call it a day:

$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done
...
...
28232
program exited with error 1

Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, we’ve run out of ports! We’re using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.

$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768    60999

Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.

  • Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).
  • Ports 1-1024 require root.
  • Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You don’t want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.
  • Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.

Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but that’s still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Let’s simply connect 15M/32k=450 new network cards to the server.

The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldn’t be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, we’ll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!

UPD. I’ve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didn’t get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Can’t we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?

Let’s use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. We’ll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:

// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it
int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]);
const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001;  // ex. 10.64.0.1
addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i);  // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2

And now we can finally finish the article.

$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done
...
...
Out of memory

Hm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would take… 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.

Runtime

By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.

TLDR: We’re using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main process’s memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.

Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, we’re doomed to build another specialised runtime. Let’s get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?

Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. What’s the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Let’s take another look at the loop.

for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) {
        if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0)
            send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        close(client);
    }

This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, we’d need to save the following state:

struct Context {
    pc: u64,        // Instruction address to return to
    fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor
    fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor
}

We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. We’re playing it safe here - we don’t need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?

$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?"
Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kb

Here’s what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.

  • 14M idle connections - 0 bytes
  • Scheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB
  • 1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GB

Only half of our RAM budget, yay! I don’t often exceed my own expectations. Let’s validate it:

int main(void) {
    // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing
    // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY!
    for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) {
        int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); 
        listen(server, 1)
    }
}
$ ./run_15m_idle_servers
Out Of Memory
$ dmesg | tail -n 1
'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?

Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. I’m not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, it’s too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - let’s dive into networking in the kernel.

Networking in the kernel

Remember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:

int main(void)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) {
        socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    }
}

That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Let’s ask AI where all the memory goes:

StructsizeofDescription
struct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeeping
struct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and padding
struct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socket
struct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeeping
Total3384B

Potato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesn’t look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. It’s Sunday and I have few tokens left, so we’ll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?

What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we can’t solve a task, we’re working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hm… level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!

The OSI model is… um… something I studied at university. Yeah, that’s a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, that’s exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?

Clear.

Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.

TCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkels’s Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.

There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:

  • gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stack
  • Seastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDB
  • lwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IP
  • F-Stack uses FreeBSD’s TCP/IP stack

Go, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but they’re nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So we’ll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:

>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for
>bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at all

So, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and can’t do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:

  • TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layer
  • TAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layer
  • DPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernel

smoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and they’re easy to use.

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() {
        Some("tun") => (
            TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?,
            Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip),
        ),
        Some("tap") => (
            TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?,
            Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()),
        ),
        _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"),
    };
    let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now());
    iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| {
        addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap();
    });
    let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new());
    
    // Main network loop
    loop {
        let now = Instant::now();
        iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets);
        wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?;
    }
}

But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: it’s common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.

DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and you’re done; when you want to read what you’ve received - it’s already there.

There’s another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but there’s a cost.

DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:

loop {
    send_from_app_memory_to_network();
    receive_from_network_to_app_memory();
}

There’s another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers can’t work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interface… it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, you’ll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.

Actually, there’s a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).

To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.

Now the final flow is:

  1. The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memory
  2. The runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by one
  3. Guest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adapters
  4. All 15M guests start listening, each on its own address
  5. The scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the next

And now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:

Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.

Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.

  • https://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers source
  • https://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDK
  • https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation site
  • https://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview
